utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we were dealing yesterday with arming of the Serbs. In the second half of 1991, did you become aware of individual cases of small amounts of weapons handed over to Serbs by individual members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to give two of the examples set out in your summary. Was there a security officer called Cedo Knezevic? If so, tell us what he did about this.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I learnt, he was in Bihac, in the counter-intelligence department, which had relocated to that locality from Zagreb, and during that period of time, the evacuation of some warehouses of the Territorial Defence was going on and the JNA from the territories that had already been under threat by the Croatian National Guard Corps, and he took a quantity - I don't know exactly how much - and he transferred it to Zemun through some route up to Batajnica, and it was planned to take it to Slavonia, but the head of security learnt about that and prevented it from taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second example, in February 1992, was there a Colonel Zecar who engaged in some provision of arms?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. He worked in the security administration, and he also was supposed to transfer a quantity of weapons, as far as I can remember now, towards Srpski Moravici. And he was uncovered in this attempt and so those weapons did not reach their destination either. He came to me and when I asked why he did that, he said that some of his superiors had ordered him to do that without me knowing, that they issued orders without me knowing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indeed identify from where his authority came?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't any written authorisations or anything like that, it was just an oral agreement, oral acquiescence from a general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you criticise the colonel or a colonel -- or, rather, this colonel for what he did? Did he identify --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just help us if you can: Did he say specifically the name of the -- I'll just see -- yes --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had done this, receiving permission from General Zivota Panic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 42. Were you aware of the particular nature of arms carried by certain paramilitary formations, and in particular, the type of automatic weapon they had?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I didn't have concrete information as to the type of weapons in the paramilitary groups, but I do remember that there was one particular type that was, nonetheless, characteristic, and it was in Slavonia, and they were the Thompson automatic weapons, which were trophy weapons mostly, and they were characterised by the fact that actually the Territorial Defence of Serbia had weapons of that kind. So most probably this type of weapon came from the warehouses of the Territorial Defence of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware of these being carried in Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia. Was this by the local Serb Territorial Defence or by paramilitary organisations or by both?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, it was paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of weapons the local Serb Territorial Defence in Eastern Slavonia were carrying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know about that. I don't have that kind of information, and I didn't have an opportunity to see for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the JNA pulled out, were you aware of what happened to some of the weapons in or leaving their warehouses?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, part of the weapons from warehouses which were not evacuated on time were taken control of by the Croatian National Guards Corps in the area, and the warehouses which were evacuated on time, the weapons were pulled out of those and taken to the territory in-depth, and part of the weaponry went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the warehouses of the JNA units that were found there at the time. And also at that time, we had larger formations being formed and larger units of the Territorial Defence in Krajina, and a part of those weapons were intended for those units, to arm those units according to the material formations that were prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the witness see tab 4 before I seek to have it admitted. I'd like to ask him a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just look at this document, General Vasiljevic, please. Remind yourself what it is, and then I'll ask you a couple of questions about it. I think it is a document with which you are personally familiar.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first receive the document or first see it, I should say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw this document sometime at the end of 1990. To be more specific, at the beginning of December 1990 when work was done to document illegal and unlawful arming, both with the Serbs and the Croats throughout Croatia and further afield as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the -- see and/or speak to the person whose statement this is, for it's a statement we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not speak to the person. The security organ in Knin talked to the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the statement shown to you in the course of your duties as being the statement of someone who had been interviewed about illegal arming?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. All this was done at the stage when the disarmament of all paramilitary -- paramilitaries was being prepared in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently find out any -- find any reason to disbelieve what this particular witness said about illegal arming in his statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. There were a number of statements, in fact, which were taken from a certain number of persons of Serb ethnicity in the Knin-Krajina area, and more or less they were identical, to all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let's deal with the admissibility of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's exactly why I was asking the questions I was, mindful of the approach that we were taking yesterday. This is a statement which contains declarations against interest by the deponent, and the part in which I am particularly interested is pages 4 and 5, and 5 in the English, starting at the words "Concerning illegal arming of citizens..." It's a contemporaneous account, as we know, because the witness saw it within days of its being prepared. He saw it in the course of his duties to investigate these matters. It's part of a body of material coming to him, he tells us, consistent in content. Never been any reason since to discount it. It is similar to the statements being put by the witness yesterday and excluded as being evidence in that it's a witness statement. There's no doubt about that. It's dissimilar in character or quality because it's not a particularly retrospective view by the witness made years after in the course of, for example, inquiries into these proceedings. It is almost as if the witness spoke to the man himself. He wasn't one of the interviewing officers; the document was handed to him afterwards. Had he been an interviewing officer with the acknowledgements or admissions by the deponent being made directly to the witness, then I would have had no difficulty at all in asking the Chamber to say it fell within the acceptable hearsay provisions of this Chamber. In this particular case, the slight difference, a couple of days between the making of the statement and the circumstances described and the witness's receiving it, places it well within the discretion of the Chamber to admit. And the events of which the deponent speaks at paragraphs on pages 4 and 5 are all, as you will see, very recent. They are between October 1990 and December of 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how is it to be distinguished from the statements which we excluded yesterday when the accused sought to put them in, records of interviews about events?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only on the grounds that I've already set out, namely that these are contemporaneous. They're clearest declarations against interest by the deponent, and they come to the -- or came to the witness in the course of his professional duties inquiring into matters at the time, which of course in certain jurisdictions is itself a factor permitting the adduction of what would otherwise be excluded hearsay. Before we move on, I just noted something in the translation that I must pursue. I'll tell you exactly what it is. You can see it on page 4. There's references to 1991 and the statement taken in 1990. I'm pretty sure that's simply an error of translation which we will be able to pick up and be able to -- Yes. I'm grateful to Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. The witness of course here in his own statement confirms the accuracy of the statement that he has made. I think the 1991 dates are simply translation errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in your opinion, you think it is not sufficient to put the content of the statement to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be my submission that it is proper for this witness to give the content of the statement in the particular circumstances in which he came first to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, of course, the deponent isn't a witness in these proceedings, so just to give him the title of witness doesn't really suit the matter that we're dealing with here. It seems to me that this falls into exactly the kind of category that we've been attempting to exclude from evidence in relation to both parties, that the production of statements made by other people who are not witnesses and then just having them put into the proceedings as exhibits. In our submission, this is not something that should happen here. There is no difference between this position and anything else that, for instance, the accused was trying to do the other day. And then you have the other statements that we've had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that be withdrawn in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll withdraw tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May tab 5 please be provided. If tab 5 of the English version could be placed on the overhead projector. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you're now looking at a document from the 1st Krajina Corps over the signature of Major General Talic, dated the 31st of August, 1992. Inventory of weapons issued in response to your confidential order, "We attach the inventory of weapons and equipment issued to units and Territorial Defence staffs, in other words, structures outside the armed forces, since the beginning of the activities aimed at protecting Serbs from genocide in Croatia and the Serbian Republic. "The weapons and equipment listed here were issued against a receipt and still figure on the ledgers of the 1st Krajina Corps units that actually issued the weapons. Please, inform us of your opinion on this matter." And then there's a schedule. If we could look at the other document, which is the schedule in English, which sets out the list of weapons and equipment issued to territorial staffs and units of the 5th Corps. And then we see guns, machine-guns, so on and so forth. Does this document fit with your account of provision of weapons or do you have any other comment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is from the 1st Krajina Corps. It dates back to August 1992, that is to say, the time when I was not an active-duty officer in the army of Yugoslavia. So I cannot really say whether it is credible and authentic or not looking at the stamp of the military post and signature of the corps commander, because I never saw his signature. However, having said that, from the list and the tables provided and the title itself, which says that it is a list of weapons and equipment issued to the TO staffs and units of the Territorial Defence from the 5th Corps -- of the 5th Corps, so this, then, was what I was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. speaking about precisely, that a part of the weaponry went from certain units, JNA units, to arm units of the Territorial Defence which at that time were being established and were formed in the different units and groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tab 6, please. Original to the witness, English version on the overhead projector. Dated the 25th of April, from the 2nd Military District Command to the MUP of the Republic of Srpska Krajina in the police station at Korenica. And the paragraph with which we are particularly concerned: "In accordance with a decision of the Federal Secretary for National Defence, top secret ... For the purpose of ammunition replenishment for the MUP of the Republika Srpska Krajina ... We issue the following ammunition to the MUP police station in Korenica from the ammunition warehouse at Golubici without any reimbursement," and then ammunition in the millions, bullets and 6.000 hand grenades and stuff of that sort, a list. Again, even if you haven't seen the document before, does this, and in particular, does the authority coming from the national -- the Federal Secretary for National Defence, SSNO, fit with your experience?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does fit, because this was a stage when, according to the Vance Plan, what was to be done was to demobilise the active components in the Kninska Krajina area and to establish the units of the Territorial Defence and the police, or milicija, whose weapons had to be kept under key and under the control of the international forces. And when those units were in fact set up and those who were to be placed under reserve composition, part of the JNA weapons were sent into the field for those units to be complete. And I should like to underline once again that we're not dealing with weapons and ammunition for the active components of the army but for reserve components in the area which would be under the control of the international forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 7, please. And the first page -- the whole document to the witness. First of all, the first page on the overhead projector, please. From the 2nd Military District Command. It's just off the top of the page. Very urgent, 24th of April, 1992. SSNO. "We have received from the Ministry of the Interior of BiH Serb Republic a request, with a strictly confidential number 11 of 23 April ... for ceding of the MTS, materiel and technical equipment, to the special purposes police detachment at the Banja Luka Security Services Centre for their needs." There's then a list of equipment, including half a dozen helicopters and items of that sort. If you go over three pages, please, Usher, to the second to last page in English. "We are sending --" the foot of the page, please. That's fine. No, the foot of that page, I think. Yes. "We are sending this request pursuant to the order of SFRY Armed Forces HQ Chief of Staff .... "We are of the opinion that these supplies have to be provided, especially those which cannot be found at the market and in the quantity that can satisfy the most basic needs." Signed by Commander Colonel General Milutin Kukanjac. And he was -- what was his position? Do you know, General?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see what the document says. Any other comment you want to make apart from what it reveals on what his position is, or does it speak for itself?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first I recognise the signature of General Kukanjac, and I recognise it on this fax copy of the document. And secondly, this is the period of time after the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina had split into two parts, because the Serb part stepped down from the MUP and formed its own MUP, the MUP of Republika Srpska, in fact. So I would say that this was a megalomaniac request in actual fact, because what is asked for are four helicopters to transport one's heavier ones, and I don't think I need to comment on this, whether it is objective or not, this request and what it asks for. But looking at this last page when this request was sent on upwards towards the General Staff of the armed forces, this actually emerges from a situation in which units of this kind and groups of this kind being established on the ground, in the field, had the practice of referring to their nearest commands for assistance for materiel and technical equipment. And what happened next would be an order from the head of the General Staff, drawing attention to the commands, that they could not immediately and directly respond to the requests made but that they would send it on up to the General Staff in Belgrade with their opinions where the final decision would be taken as to each individual request separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Be that as it may, what we see here is that this is assisting in the arming of Bosnian Serbs; is that right? Just yes or no. Well, no -- yes. This is arming the Bosnian Serbs and indeed ...

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not hearing the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think actually the document speaks for itself and I'll move on. The next exhibit is an intercept which has already been produced. It was Exhibit 353, tab 39, between Karadzic and the accused, dated the 23rd of September, 1991. There is the declaration that is produced from this witness. Your Honour, I'm not going to take the time dealing again with the content of that intercept. If it may be produced, the declaration. Tab 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you listen to an intercept, General, identified here Exhibit 353 tab 39, were you able to identify the voices on it as the voices identified of Karadzic and the accused?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to several conversations where I was able to identify the voices and to evaluate the content of the conversation. I don't know which specific conversation you are referring to now, but the ones that were shown to me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the ones there. You'll see one of them is Exhibit 353, tab 39, and the voices are registered there. And you signed the declaration accordingly.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is nothing contentious here. All the conversations listed on this document, I looked at the originals and I confirm that I made this statement so that there should be no problem here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we move now, then, to the training of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will perhaps play a couple of intercepts but no more. As to the balance, we'll either just have the witness confirm his identification of the voices where the material has already been considered or occasionally give a summary of what he knows from those intercepts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can we move to the obtaining of volunteers. Did the security administration learn of Frenki Simatovic in the Krajina area, and if so, when and to what effect?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the first information that arrived, and it was sometime in the autumn of 1990. We did not have full identifying data at the time, we just knew about the name Frenki and the presence of this person in the Krajina area and that at that time he was an employee of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn of a man called Captain Dragan, and if so, what did you learn of him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, Captain Dragan turned up in Knin sometime in early 1991. He trained volunteers from the Knin Krajina in a camp or a facility in Golubici. Quite a lot of time elapsed before his identity was established, and according to the information that was later fully confirmed, he arrived from Australia with the help and mediation of the people from the State Security Service of Serbia, and he was one of their sources, apparently. This is as far as training in the Krajina is concerned. When I was in Sid on the 28th of October, 1991, in connection with determining the circumstances surrounding the crime committed in that village, I had a short briefing with the security organs of the time from the 1st Military District, which was located in Sid. [redacted]. On that occasion, he told me that in the area of Sid and further afield there were several volunteer paramilitary units which were not under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army and that there was some camps where these volunteers were received and trained, and it was not known where they went after their training and who sent them there. One of these camps was the Lipovaca camp which, as far as he knew, had about a hundred volunteers. Some of his senior officers from the security sector where he was tried to reach the camp, but they were not admitted. They were not allowed to enter. Mirko Jovic's unit was there, which bore the name Dusan Silni and which perpetrated the crimes in Lovas directly. Then there was also a detachment which was referred to as Crnogorac or Montenegrin. It was a mobile detachment with several vehicles, and it moved from one area to another. The people behind this detachment were from the MUP. As far as he knew, Radovan Stojicic Badza was in charge of it. He then told me that in Erdut there was a unit commanded by Raznjatovic, Arkan, and the status of that unit shifted continually. The number of men ranged from several dozen to 200 or 300 men. As far as I can recall, it was a special purpose police unit commanded by Vasilije Mijovic. That was another unit. And this unit operated later on in the Baranja area, and it had a camp on a farm near Sombor. That's what I can remember from that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the only detail that we'll probably get elsewhere but just take it now; Captain Dragan's training centre was near Knin at what town or village?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Golubic near Knin. I mentioned that. I said it was in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My error for overlooking it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into closed session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what happened when reservists were called up in Serbia for the JNA and what the accused's attitude to the call-up of reservists and the use of volunteers was.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia, there were obvious problems about the response of reservists in 1991. A large number of wartime JNA units could not be established, and some who were established, although with a lot of problems, soon disintegrated. At that time, the slogan that was bandied around in Serbia and put forward through the media was that Serbia was not at war, and as far as I can remember, the accused used to say that we would not force anyone to go to war. And from this it followed that only those who wanted to would join the JNA. The practical consequences of this in the field was a large number of deserters whom the MUP did not want to arrest or bring to the units, which they were bound to do under the law, and this opened up room for various volunteer groups which often had the characteristics of a particular political party, and they would be mobilised to enhance the political image of the parties at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on, at the same time as there were these difficulties with call-ups or with what might be determined draft-dodgers, I'm not sure, was the Territorial Defence of Serbia making any offers for the provision of troops to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I attended a meeting in the Ministry of Defence of Serbia in late October 1991 where there was discussion, among other things, of the poor response to the call-up and the poor replenishment of the JNA units with men. And then the commander of the Territorial Defence said they were not having any problems at all with replenishing the Territorial Defence units and that some Territorial Defence units could be sent and used where this was needed. Whether this was an official proposal, I don't know, but I do know that some territorial units from Serbia were at the Slavonian battlefield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to -- as you told us really yesterday, the authority to use Territorial Defence units in that way could ultimately only come from whom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think only the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, just to tidy up something that I understated yesterday when we were talking about the Lika authority -- this is paragraph 24, Your Honour; I may have left things unclear -- when we were talking about the Lika authority that would be required to use territorial detachments in Valjevo, in Lovas, or of territorial units from Montenegro in Kordun, in fact is it your evidence that such deployments did take place and therefore would have required the authority of the same president?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that these units were in these areas that you have mentioned, and I said that I assume and that it is my opinion that such a decision would have been under the competence of the president of the republic, because this is a category or, rather, an area in which I am not an expert. I don't know what the powers of the president of the republic are, but I do know in principle that he is the Commander in Chief and that, in principle, he should issue the approval for such a deployment of units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning, then, to what you were saying about volunteers being linked to political parties - paragraph 48 - were there for a short period of time centres, two of them in Serbia, for the training of volunteers, one at Smederavska Palanka and another in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were centres that the JNA tried to organise so that volunteers would be received and dealt with in accordance with the regulations. These centres, however, have operated for only a short time, and I remember the incident that took place at the centre in Palanka, because I received a report that people were coming there wearing party insignia, that they were unkempt, that they wore beards, that they refused to put on JNA uniforms and carry the insignia that were then prescribed, and that they set themselves apart as compact units, and they also caused mischief; they went out to town and broke shop windows owned by Albanians, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so was it the case that those two centres didn't last for very long?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move now to the Serb Territorial Defence in Croatia at the time which you can help us with. And if we can use the term "Eastern Slavonia" for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, can you tell us, please, did you detect differences between the operation of the Territorial Defence in the Krajina and in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, in the Krajina, the Territorial Defence was established pursuant to the then-valid principles governing the establishment of staffs and units. This meant that the commanders of the staffs, the Territorial Defence staffs, were mostly active-duty officers. In specific terms, I know that in the Knin Krajina a number of senior officers, through the personnel department, were assigned to duties as commanders of the Territorial Defence units. I will mention one, that was General Djuic, who was appointed commander of a Territorial Defence Staff. These units were subordinated to the JNA units operating there. In contrast to this, in Eastern Slavonia I do not know of any active-duty JNA senior officers being appointed as commanders of any Territorial Defence staffs in Eastern Slavonia. Even those who -- who had been performing these duties up to the beginning of the war in Eastern Slavonia were replaced. I know of one such replacement, both of the commander and the Chief of Staff and the security officer in the Territorial Defence Staff in Sid. So that in Eastern Slavonia, there were legal Territorial Defence units. One of the people who led the Territorial Defence units, as far as I can recall, was General Mandaric, who was at the forward command post of the 1st Military District together with General Zivota Panic, which was quite natural, because in an operation of that kind, it was normal to have coordination of activities between the JNA units and the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Couple of details just to flesh that out: You've spoken of General Djuic who was, I think, an active JNA officer appointed commander of the Krajina Territorial Defence, and I think you said probably appointed by the personnel administration, but I'll just check that, if I can. But the appointment of --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- a general to that position required the authority of whom, of what level?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. During -- objection. Mr. Nice is conducting the examination of this witness wrongfully, because during Babic's testimony, it was shown that he appointed this Djuic, who had previously been retired, who was a retiree, on his own. So he was not appointed by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence at all. And now he is asking the witness what is the rule when the JNA appoints generals. It has to be someone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness give the evidence of what he knows. He will not be led by counsel. He will merely give the evidence from what he knows and understands. Let him do that. Mr. Nice will not lead him. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What level and by whom, as you understood it, would General Djuic have been appointed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Djuic was in the inspectorate of the armed forces of the SFRY. Generals are appointed to any post by the Presidency of Yugoslavia, by their own decree. And as far as I can remember, from the inspectorate of the armed forces, he was transferred to Krajina. Whether his status was changed in the service before that is something that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So appointment by the Presidency of the -- of Yugoslavia by their own decree, that would be ultimately - or perhaps consequentially - over whose signature would you expect such an appointment to be authorised?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the president of the Presidency or somebody acting on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who that was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little more detail. So far as Eastern Slavonia is concerned - and you may have mentioned this and I missed it - you've given an account of how you think it was set up. Did you actually see any documentation supporting your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to what is written down on the 28th of October in my notebook, my working notebook, these were personnel changes carried out in the staff of the Territorial Defence in Sid. I remember on the 25th of February, 1992, there was a meeting held in Vukovar between General Zivota Panic, General Mandaric, Jovica Stanisic, Radovan Stojicic Badza, and Goran Hadzic. New commanders were appointed at that meeting, new commanders of the Territorial Defence Staff in Vukovar. As I was informed by the security organ, the persons appointed to these positions were two officials -- I mean until then, two officials of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pausing for one minute there, please, General. You're giving detail, and I realise that you're still at an early stage of the evidence. Is this material you're happy to give in open session or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I can. That's no problem for me. That part I can present that way. So Branko Curcic was appointed, and another man whose name I cannot recall right this moment. So in this way, people from the MUP, from the MUP of Serbia, were appointed as commanders of the Territorial Defence staff in Vukovar. It would have been natural to appoint military personnel or military experts, because that was the prevalent practice otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, I think, on this topic, did you observe the presence of groups such as Dusan Silni, and did that mark any difference in the operations in Krajina from the operations in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were such attempts made by certain parties from Serbia to send larger groups of volunteers to Krajina. I know that on the ground that was something that was not received gladly, so that every attempt was made to have them returned. There was a larger group coming from the Serbian Renewal Movement, for example, and it is known that two of the main persons from that detachment got killed in Krajina. However, they were not on a rampage, so to speak, these so-called volunteer units that were not under the command of the Territorial Defence or the army. At least, they could not hold out for long as such. As opposed to that, in Eastern Slavonia the situation was quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, there are a couple more details before we perhaps go into closed session, with the Chamber's leave. You've spoken of General Mandaric, who was the commander of the regular Territorial Defence of Vojvodina being present at the forward command post, I think. Was that in the military facility at Karadjordjevo in the town of Mladenovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mladenovo could be called a town, but anyway, that is the locality, the one that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that he was there regularly or irregularly? And if he was there regularly, what significance if any was there in that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was regular because there were Territorial Defence units from Vojvodina and because at that time he was commander of the Territorial Defence of Vojvodina. So he was directly with the commander of the 1st Military District, and in that way operations were coordinated among the Territorial Defence units and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had there been a regular and fully effective Territorial Defence in place in Eastern Slavonia, would you have expected this level of attendance by General Mandaric?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the specific situation. It is not unusual. As a matter of fact, it is desirable for two commanders to be together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may have mentioned a unit called Sajkaska Brigade, and if you haven't -- I may have missed it, but if you haven't mentioned it, what did you learn of them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mentioned that by way of an illustration, that Territorial Defence units of Vojvodina were in the area of Eastern Slavonia. So when I talked about these legal units, that is the name of a particular Territorial Defence unit. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go briefly into closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, was there a meeting on the 25th of February of 1992 in Erdut -- sorry. I'm told you covered that already. It's my mistake for not registering that and moving too fast. Just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry I wasn't able to tick off paragraph 58.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I think you may have covered some of it or most of it. There was a meeting on the 25th of February, 1992, in Erdut, attended by whom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that what was discussed were the appointments in the Territorial Defence Staff of Vukovar, that General Zivota Panic was there, General Mandaric, Jovica Stanisic, Radovan Stojicic Badza, and Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, what decision was made about who was to be the commander of the Territorial Defence in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've said already that two men were appointed from the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've identified at this part of the summary the map Exhibit 327, tab 12, which has already been tendered, which may be a useful map for the Chamber to have to hand for geographical references.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move to another short closed session, General, a very short one, you, I think, regard there is some significance in the treatment that was accorded you different from the treatment accorded Arkan when you visited the Serbian Ministry of Defence. Can you just explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I can. At the entrance into the Ministry of Defence, although I was wearing my field uniform, I was asked at the entrance, at the office there, to leave my weapons because that was in accordance with regulations. That was strange in view of the time and in view of the fact that I was wearing field uniform. And I knew that Raznjatovic came to that same ministry to attend meetings at somebody's office and that he walked in with a Heckler, with an automatic rifle. I reacted: "Why am I being disarmed as a general and Arkan walks in with an automatic weapon?" And this man answered quite simply, "Well, you're not Arkan."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I gather that the reference to the map was an incorrect reference. I'll tidy that up later.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 326, tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I apologise for the error. A short closed session, if registry could accommodate us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were still head of UB, did you discover any connection between the recruitment of volunteers and political parties? You've touched on this already. Interested with your comment or observation on anything that Seselj said about this.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what you're asking now is a well-known fact where I live. Specifically as regards the involvement of the members of the Radical Party in these volunteer units that were sent to the Slavonian theatre of war, I remember a BBC television programme called "The Death of Yugoslavia," in which Mr. Seselj said quite openly that he was engaged by Jovica Stanisic to rally volunteers and that he got weapons from the state security service for arming them. It is quite noticeable that no one from the MUP ever denied that, so his statement is probably a truthful one. Otherwise, on the ground, I did have knowledge that there was a group of radicals that consisted of the members of the Radical Party, and that detachment was called Leva Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this may be a convenient moment. Before I forget, there is one matter on which we are awaiting a response from the Prosecution, and it relates to the large number of documents which the accused says has been disclosed on him during the period before we started sitting again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It hasn't been overlooked. Inevitably, Ms. Dicklich, who is heavily engaged in court and out of court until all hours, has also to supervise the preparation of this document. We are preparing it at the same time as we are preparing a general Rule 68 report, because another one is due, and I think they'll both be with you, I think, by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 387, tab 10, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 387, tab 10, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at it very briefly and then followed by tab 11. The English translation is somewhat incomplete because of the quality of the handwritten original, but, General Vasiljevic, is this a letter dated the 10th of August, 1991, coming from someone called Branislav Vakic? And the content of the letter is to this effect: Written to the military post at Baosici, and it says: On the 6th of July, in accordance with an order, a T-1, registration number K-5459 was given to the Serbian Radical Party unit currently deployed in Grab. The name of the unit is Serbian Volunteers, something to that effect, and is part of the Hercegovina Corps under the command of a colonel whose name isn't quite legible. Then it says, P-4463 has remained in the unit so as to be fixed and then replaced. On the 10th of August, in accordance with General, whoever it may be, a PG-4463 was given, on the condition that something be returned by the command of Serbian Volunteers of Herzegovina, a Chetnik major. Signed Branislav Vakic. If we can then look at tab 11 very briefly, please. Is this something called a trip ticket, and it deals with an official travel report validity for a Pinzgauer, consumption of fuel, but importantly, we note that the driver is the same; one of them is Branislav Vakic. These two documents, then, please, General, at tabs 10 and 11, what do they show us in respect of what you were telling us earlier about political parties and volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first document, either it's been wrongly translated or not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. properly stated, but it was a document dating to August 1992, and I think you said 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and it's obviously just an error of translation.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From both these documents, we can see that the units which were sent by some parties, political parties from Serbia, to the areas, in this case in Montenegro, relied upon the JNA commands from which they received either vehicles or were able to tank up for fuel purposes at the army petrol stations. And I know that Branislav Vakic, in fact, was a member of the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 62. To what extent had the DB of Serbia infiltrated political parties of the opposition at this time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security, the DB of Serbia, had very good positions in practically all the opposition parties of the day, and it was well-informed about the overall situation within them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did it -- to whom was it directly subordinate, the state security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To all intents and purposes, it was subordinated to the President of Serbia at the time, that is to say Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the information on opposition parties available to the state security, in your judgement, would it have been available to him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would have to have been, because no service collecting information collects information for itself, for its own purposes but it is duty-bound and obliged to inform the person who is superior to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he became President of the FRY, what was the position then about the DB of Serbia? To whom was it then subordinate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a very short space of time, it was to be subordinated contrary to the provisions in force at the time. Once again, subordinated to President Milosevic as the president of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 63, Your Honour, is one I'm just going to take a little -- the paragraphs ceased to be numbered for a few paragraphs, but I'm going to take a little context at the foot of page 11 and one paragraph on page 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, was there an admiral called Mamula who had both political and, as it were, military interests?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was General Mamula. As to an answer whether he had military interests and political ones too, you would have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he known to you to have any particular political interest or interest in any particular political party? If not, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes, I know what you mean. You want me to speak to the period, that is to say, when Mamula was the Federal Secretary for National Defence or, rather, when Admiral Mamula was a retired admiral. So I assume what you're interested in is the latter period, when General Mamula was retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he had retired, for a time - and that was in 1991, in the summer - he held high-ranking posts in the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, the movement for Yugoslavia, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I need for that. And then we move on page 12, top of the page. Was there a meeting he sought with you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And this was in the summer months. I think it was the end of July or perhaps the beginning of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you decline to meet him yourself but ask your deputy, General Tumanov, to see him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't refuse. I would prefer the term I avoided meeting him, because there had already been a slight conflict or clash, if I can put it that way, between General Kadijevic and Admiral Mamula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, did General Tumanov meet him, and did he report back to you on what the admiral had sought?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He had a brief meeting, and he told me that it was the admiral's interest in seeing that some of the security officers or staff of the security administration should be sent into the area of Lika, Banija, and Kordun to provide security to the units over there, the units that had been established, units of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this something the state security then did or declined to do?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're thinking of military security, are you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation I got was "state security."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military security. Your units, did they provide officers pursuant to this request?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 65, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It couldn't have gone forward without permission from me, and I did not grant permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 28th of November of 1991, did you speak to your superior, Kadijevic, about paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and previously the -- General Kadijevic and the leadership had been sent information about the presence of the paramilitary groups on the territory of Slavonia. And to be more specific, the reason for in-depth monitoring and reporting were the problems that had been created after the goings-on in Vukovar. And some volunteer groups insisted, those which were not within the frameworks of the JNA, insisted that they be paid a remuneration that was due them. And as this was not accepted, because they weren't on the lists of JNA members, they resorted to various excessive situations. And we had information that after the operation in Vukovar was over, these groups went about looting, looting from the houses that had been abandoned. And for that reason, General Kadijevic issued orders that orders be issued to disband and disarm all the paramilitary formations from the areas where military units were present. This order came out on the 10th of December, as far as I recall, 1991, and it was issued by the Presidency in restricted composition, that is to say, the Yugoslav state Presidency of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 12 of Exhibit 387, please. We need look at no more than the top of the first page where the "Order on the engagement of volunteers in the armed forces of the SFRY during immediate danger of war" is headlined. And then if we go over to the second page, paragraph 7, we read: "Volunteer formations currently engaged outside the Armed Forces of the SFRY on the carrying out of certain military assignments and volunteers currently in the units and institutions of the Armed Forces of the SFRY must bring their position [something] the armed forces of the SFRY into accord with the regulations in this order within --" I'm not sure how many days it is. It looks like 30. How many days is it, General?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know how many days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 of the order, and in the original -- it's ten days. Ten days of the order. And this is the order signed by Branko Kostic that you were telling us about.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never saw it before, but I see it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Arkan's group comply with this order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan's group did not comply with this order, and I know that from the reports -- a report sent in to me via the 1st Military District, in fact, from Colonel Petkovic. In concrete terms, on the 28th of January, 1992, General Zivota Panic ordered Colonel Petkovic to come into contact with Radovan Stojicic, nicknamed Badza, from the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, and to caution him, to warn him that Arkan's units had to leave the areas where the military units were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- carry on with Badza's response, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badza's response was the following: He said that there would be no problem with Arkan's Tigers. He would take them over within the composition of the unit being established by the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A short closed session, please -- private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1 [redacted] 2 [redacted] 3 [redacted] 4 [redacted] 5 [redacted]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we talk about something -- or can you talk about something quite briefly called operational groups, OGs, in a couple of sentences. And remembering what you told us yesterday about the concept of unity or singleness of command, how did operational groups come into being and operate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operational groups, according to the rules, are formed when several units of different kinds, which are not from the same organic composition, act on a common task and a common area, in the same area. In order to ensure efficient command and carrying out of the task and to reduce the number of direct links with the commander, operational groups are established and the lower level category are tactical groups. Therefore, an operational group is a term normally employed in military terminology, and I know that in the area of Banija, Lika, and Kordun, three JNA operational groups were set up, the 5th, 6th -- rather, the 7th and the -- 6th, 7th, and 8th Operational Groups, and there was one in the Slavonia area as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who would have authority to create an operational group comprising JNA as well as Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the commander of the military district who creates an operational group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: English on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This from Major General Spiro Nikovic. Territorial Defence, Socialist Republic of Croatia, 19th of October, 1991, 1st Operational Group Command, heading: Placing Territorial Defence Units Under JNA Units. The order, and then perhaps the second paragraph: "All TD units --" Territorial Defence units -- "from the territorial zone headquarters of Banija and Kordun ... are placed under 1st Operational group Command starting on 19th October... and continue as such to be engaged and used as an organic part of JNA units in the combat zones where JNA units are." This is simply an example of the creation of an operational group that you've spoken of.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is an example of resubordination of Territorial Defence units from the area staff of the Banija and Kordun to the command of the operational group, who is Spiro Nikovic. So he had to receive an order on the establishment of an operational group in which he would be told that this area staff of the Territorial Defence would be resubordinated to him. And on the basis of this command, he would have received from the military district command, he would have issued an order to the area command and to these units, telling them that they are now under his command. So this is not an organisational order on the formation of an operational group. Rather, it is an order issued to these units, informing them that, from now on, they are under his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I follow that. It was my error. This reflects the existence of an operational group in the way that you've described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have it, we can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at tab 14, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see this on the overhead projector. Not all of it has been translated, but this is a letter going to Comrade Martic, and so far as material, it reads: "The Federal Department --" to the Ministry of SAO Krajina and to Milan Martic. "The Federal Department for National Defence ordered me to come, together with a group of superiors on the specific day to Vrhovine and to make preparations for establishing the 2nd Lika's brigade of the 6th Lika's division that will take over the commanding from the Territorial Defence and that will combine activities of all structures on this territory." Now, does this explain the creation of the Lika Brigade and the combination of all activities in that area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that sometime in August 1991, at a meeting with the Secretary for National Defence, General Kadijevic, a decision was reached on the establishment of the 6th Lika Division. And from that it follows that these brigades were also formed. And this is within the context of what I said, that these were not paramilitary units but units under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is very helpfully covering something that had I omitted at paragraph 52. And the commander of this unit --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if this is an objection, we'll hear it, but it shouldn't interrupt too much. Now, what is the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In essence, Mr. May, in tab 14, this letter written to Martic by Trbojevic, in the English translation, only one paragraph has been translated. The original is a whole page. And you cannot determine anything. And he's complaining about a paramilitary formation and saying that they were common thieves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will deal with it in this way: Mr. Nice, can we have the whole letter translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on its way, yes. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But returning to the topic of the creation of this division or brigade out of the 6th Division, you were telling us, General, about the decision of General Kadijevic. The units of the JNA, paragraph 52 for reference. Who was the commander of the division?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I have to explain why the 6th Lika Division was established, if you will permit me. After the reorganisation of the JNA in 1987, this area objectively had no large JNA units there. And as war was beginning, there was a need to establish or reactivate those units which had existed previously, before 1987. And this -- it was in this context that the order was issued to establish the 6th Lika Division. I don't know who the commander was, but I know that Mica Cusic, an active duty general, was commanded to go to the area and assist the commands there in establishing the units. I don't know, however, who was appointed commander of this unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cusic was, of course, a JNA officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a general of the JNA. And he was still on active-duty service at the time. He was available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 72, please. I want to turn to the support of the JNA, to the armies of Krajina and the Republika Srpska. Can you tell us, please, this: From mid-1992 until the end of the conflict, what number of officers of the VJ, as you discovered, served in the SVK and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, are we now in open session, to remind you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very grateful. At the foot of the page, and -- yes, please, may we go into closed session? I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're now in open session, General. Either the end of April or the beginning of May 1992, did the Rump Presidency make a decision about officers of the JNA born in Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina and as to where they should serve?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this decision was made pursuant to a conversation between Branko Kostic and Blagoje Adzic with President Izetbegovic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Skopje on the 26th of April, 1992. An agreement was reached on that occasion that all members of the JNA who were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina should remain in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that Muslims and other citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina within a fixed period of time and that all the senior officers and soldiers who were not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina would leave Bosnia and Herzegovina within a certain time period. As far as I remember, the deadline for withdrawal to Yugoslavia was the 19th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: English version on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This comes, as we'll see, from the chief of the staff of the armed forces at the headquarters of the armed forces operative centre to the command of the 5th, 10th, 13th, and 17th Corps and the 4th Military Region, and for information, the 2nd Military Region, and it reads: "On Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the basis of the entire situation on the territory of the Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in accordance with the decision of the SFRJ on the transfer of members of the JNA - citizens of SRJ from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the territory of SRJ, and vice versa, "I am issuing the order: "Carry out all the necessary preparations and transfer the following..." And if we go to the second page, paragraphs 2 and 3: "The officers, soldiers and civilians from the aforesaid units born in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Krajina, that is, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or according to the plan of the Personnel Department of the Federal Department for National Defence are determined for the reinforcement of the Territorial Defence and the police of the Serbian Republic of Krajina or the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, will stay in the territory." And then a further order. Comment on this document, please, General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is in accordance with what I have already said. And the deadline of the 19th of May, units and personnel who are citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are being transferred. There is one thing that is insufficiently clear to me here. Under item 2, when it says: "According to the plan of the personal administration of the SSNO, they are to bring up to manpower levels the Krajina Territorial Defence and police." I assume that this means that the citizens from the Krajina and Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were active-duty members of the JNA and who were to be transferred to the Krajina and Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they were to be appointed according to the plan of the personnel administration, because this document was issued on the 11th of May when I had already retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 16. We look at this. This is a document much later, the 7th of December of 1993. And I needn't trouble the usher to turn to it, but we can find in due course that it comes from Major General Mile Novakovic, and it's a list of military personnel who left the Serbian army of Krajina without permission, and it goes, amongst others, to Lieutenant General Perisic. And the document says: "In our document, confidential number ... submitted to you a list of officers who left the Serbian army of Krajina without permission and returned to the Yugoslav army." And then: "We hereby inform you that the following persons replied to our summons." And then in the middle of the page: "We ask you take necessary measures for return to the SVK of those who did not reply to our summons and whose names we send you again ..." And then there's a long list. What does this help us with, General? Any comment on this document as to the way personnel support was organised?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this supports everything I have said up to now. There was an intervention in order for members of the army of Yugoslavia who were born in the Krajina, or in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not remain in the units in the field, and so an appeal is made to the Chief of Staff that he should use his authority to return these people to the army of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we see that there had already been an earlier list submitted and non-compliance with that list so that this was further pressure or enforcement. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're still in open session, remember. Later on - you may have covered this but just detail it very briefly if you will - it was also citizens as well as the military who were ordered to serve in the army of the Krajina or Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in this document here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Forget the document. No, we're moving on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both. Both. There was some sort of mobilisation in the area of the Republic of Yugoslavia where all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina or Croatia who had not responded to the call that they should report to the army of their republic or Krajina be rounded up. And they were on the territory of Yugoslavia. And the other case was if they were active members of the army of Yugoslavia, they were put into a situation where they had to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've covered paragraphs 75 and 76 in one setting or another. So far as 77 is concerned, perhaps a sentence from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, were promotions of officers in the SVK or VRS sometimes upheld when they returned to the VJ? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the interpretation was not right. I assume you mean promotion to higher rank --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the army of the Krajina or the republic. If that is what you meant, and I think you did, then on their return - I'm referring to senior officers who after a certain period of time returned from the Krajina or the Republika Srpska to the army of Yugoslavia - their ranks had to be verified by the competent organs in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I know of some cases where some ranks to which they had been promoted were not upheld, although in the army of the Krajina or of Republika Srpska, they had already -- these ranks had already been conferred upon them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your experience, did officers in the SVK or VRS maintain contact with their VJ units and the commanders of those units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I experienced this myself because I contacted some of them. I was in contact with some of them. It's as if these were people who were temporarily assigned outside the army of Yugoslavia. And since their families lived in Yugoslavia, they came to visit them, and then they had occasion of having informal contact with their previous superior officers. They were probably asking whether their previous posts were taken up and whether there would be any possibility for them to come back there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, the support that you've described, the VJ to the SVK and the VRS, how did that, in your judgement, reflect as to whether these were entirely separate armies or whether they were in some ways connected?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the factual situation, these were two states that had two armies, and they were financed from a third state. I don't know whether there is any need for clarifying this in order to make it clearer. So there is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There are the two Krajinas or, rather, the Krajina and the Republika Srpska who have their own governments, who have their own armies, but the funding comes from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We may be dealing with that later in a different session in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 16, for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But staying with the measure of personnel support and accepting that these armies were based in different countries, did they operate to any extent as if they were based in the same country or did they operate as if they were truly and completely based in different countries?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the specific operations, I cannot speak authoritatively about that, so I cannot give a precise answer to that question. If you mean who commanded which army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I don't mean that, and what I'm going to do is come back to it a little later. Let's look, please, now, if we can, at Exhibit 327, tab 23. This is, of course, after your retirement, but I would be grateful for your comment on this and some other documents. This is a letter of the 9th of June, and it comes from Milan Martic, Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and it says, going as it does to the accused: "Dear Mr. President: "Having assessed the military and political situation in the Republic of Serbian Krajina as very complex, we feel obliged to inform you about it and --" I'm so sorry. "We feel obliged to inform you about it and to ask you to use your authority and position to improve the situation." We go over to the second page and to the bottom of the page, please. "The SRJ army failed to meet its obligations regarding the required ammunition and spare parts. "We hereby ask you to do the following: "To exert pressure on the General Staff of the Yugoslav army to provide us with the required ammunition, spare parts ... "Serbian television should report on Croatia's intentions in the media, and include news from the RSK in the evening news headlines. It would be advisable to send a Serbian television crew to the front of Northern Dalmatia if possible. "The GS of the Yugoslav army should send the requested officers to RSK." And over the page. Next page, please. "It's worth noting that we've sent these requests to the chief of the Yugoslav army, but they are being fulfilled slowly or not at all." As to the integration of working together as different armies on different territories, what, if anything, do you have to say by way of comment about this letter?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This last section that you read, it would be natural if Mr. Martic would, in relation to the problems he had in his communications with the army of Yugoslavia, address the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who is in charge of commanding the army of Yugoslavia. If he addresses the person he did address, at that time he was just one of the members of the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, so it would be natural for this to be sent to the other member of the Supreme Defence Council of Yugoslavia. So he is actually addressing here the person who he believes has factual influence and who can issue orders through the General Staff for granting Martic's requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then two topics covered, the nature of the help that was expected or sought and the fact that the letter goes to the accused. Can we look then now, please - perhaps the same topics in mind - to Exhibit 327, tab 5. This one from Goran Hadzic, president of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. Received on the 24th of June, 1993. So again, outside the period of your engagement when you were in retirement. To the president of the Republic. "Dear Mr. Milosevic: "We want to draw your attention to certain problems which we were not able to solve by ourselves ... and which represent the urgent problems of the Serbian army of Krajina." Next paragraph: " ... asking for military personnel procurement and so on." Next paragraph: "Technical maintenance of weapons." Next paragraph: "Minimal ammunition." And then next paragraph but one: "We ask you to try to exercise your authority and influence for realisation of our requests presented to the General Staff of the Yugoslav army." This was addressed to the accused. Do the comments you made in relation to the previous letter apply similarly to this one?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 17, please. The first page, please, on the overhead projector. This is a SitRep, a situation report, on the 25th of November. We can see it goes to the office of the president and the president personally and to the Chief of Staff, General Perisic. And then if we go on to the third page, please, usher, to paragraph 2.3. "Mobilisation and Personnel Issues: "There have been no major changes since the last report. "A new group of active-duty military personnel arrived from the VJ on the 23rd of November ... "Of the 259 called up, 82 responded, i.e., 31 per cent." The problem with the lack of doctors. And then this is signed by Borislav Djukic. Your comment on this document that comes from the Serbian Krajina army Main Staff, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is in the context of sending officers of the army of Yugoslavia to the army of Republika Srpska Krajina. And again, there is this intervention which is in accordance with the documents you showed beforehand, that those who had not responded to the call-up should Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. respond. And the chief of General Staff is informed about this and also the Supreme Defence Council.
