This is yet another document in this respect, and it shows where the Main Staff of the army of the Serb Republic of Krajina, where the Main Staff is vis-a-vis the army of Yugoslavia. It would be interesting now to see later whether something was done in connection with these interventions, that is to say, to send those who had not responded earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally in this series of exhibits, tab 18, please. 25th of May, document from the Serbian Interior Ministry over an illegible signature but with a stamp on the original. Subject: To approve certificate. "This is to approve the transfer from Skelane of the following commodities seized as war bounty in territories where combat operations are taking place." Some minor items listed. "The certificate is being issued on the basis of the Order of the Tactical Group Commander, General Mile Mrksic ..." Your comment on this document coming from the Republika Srpska covering war booty, signed by Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing that is evident is that the unit for special purposes of the MUP of the Serbia, in May 1993, had its command in Bajna Basta. However, there is another thing that can be seen, that television, typewriter, a stove, a water heater are being transferred from Skelane which is the Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is obvious that this unit operated in that area. As for the existence of Tactical Group 1 commanded by General Mrksic, it is there, and he issued an order as to how war booty should be treated. I'm not aware of this existence of Tactical Group 1. I am not aware of that. This is 1993, but the document is -- makes this quite evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to touch 79 or tab 19. May we have a short closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is now a full English translation of tab 14. I hope it's been included in your -- oh, it hasn't. So we now will be in the position of the accused and the witness, able to read the document in full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn then to logistical support, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Nice. Paragraph 82, if the witness can deal with the name UB. It's written here "UB/KOS," so whether it should be read "KOG" and the distinction between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: KOS, KOG, and UB, yes. I'll ask the witness about that. It may be that we'll want to look at one of our charts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any event, so far as you're concerned, General, what did KOS ever mean? When did it cease to be an appropriate current term?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour looks at this chart - I can't remember the number of it - the JNA command structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 1. In the legend in the bottom left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] KOS, in translation, means counter-intelligence service of the JNA. And it ceased to exist in the 1950s. The official term, the official title or name was the Security Administration of the JNA or the Organs of Security of the JNA, and KOS does not actually exist as an expression any more, as a term. It is synonymous with the security organs, but we don't use it in ordinary life, even less in official communication. The KOG, KOG, stands for counter-intelligence group, and this is a branch of the security organs which has specific counter-intelligence assignments. So KOG is a component part of the security organs or, as it says KOG, counter-intelligence group. And it has its own branches, counter-intelligence branches, and those are the official names or titles of those organisational entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- this is covered in the summary. We were probably not going to deal with it simply for the usual problems of time, but you'll see it on page 28, and there's a tab 36 that may help, but it may be we can turn to the need to spend time on that when we reach that part of the summary. You will find a rather detailed chart at tab 36, and we will review the position between now and next Wednesday as to how much of that we should give.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 20, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could place it on the overhead projector. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're on the topic of logistical support, General, and we've got here a document of the 31st of December, 1991, so back within your period. Equipping Territorial Defence units coming from the SSNO. Equipping Territorial Defence units with weapons and military equipment. And it says: "Since the start of combat operations, territorial operation Territorial Defence units that have been formed have contacted the SSNO directly, either themselves or through their staffs, to request replenishment --" it's at the top of the page, Usher. "... staffs, to request replenishment of NVO weapons and materiel equipment from JNA. "When conditions allowed, these units were equipped by the relevant tactical bodies SNO arms and services through the 608 something or other of the SSNO and the VO command. Due to the large number of requests and the difficulties involved in continuing to meet the level of the SSNO and in order to continue to observe regulations and prevent potential abuse, I order..." And then chief of the General Staff, Adzic orders: "Replenishment of Territorial Defence units in accordance with regulations." Sorry. Have I got the wrong document? I'm so sorry. Apparently I'm reading from the wrong document. Very well. Sorry. As you were, if people wonder what I was reading from, this is the one that's pursuant to an order 2260, Chief of the General Staff orders in respect of regulations and possible abuse during the equipping of Territorial Defence units, orders replenishing the Territorial Defence units in accordance with regulations in force. Item 2: Analysing requests received and assess whether they're warranted. After those tactically responsible are given approval, SSNO will prepare decisions. Corps and logistics base commands must inform those from this command who are tactically responsible and then hand over allocated equipment to the commands and staffs of the TO units. That came -- that was tab 20. Thank you very much. I hope that the Judges -- the Court's binders are tabbed in the way that I've now understood. 21, then. Let's see if I've got 21. Can we put -- I think the better thing is for you to comment straight away on tab 20, please, General. What does this tell us, 1992 January, about the logistical support of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document comes from an order of the General Staff head dating back to December 1991, and all this is taking place during a period of time when, according to the Vance Plan, the JNA should be leaving Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. certain areas. And the weapons, military materiel and TO units should be placed under the control of the international forces. And it is during this period of time that replenishment is taking place and additional arming. And some units of the Territorial Defence, according to this, probably did not have all the technical means and materiel they should have been equipped with. As previously, we already said that some Territorial Defence units and the MUP of Republika Srpska itself would make direct requests to the commands in the field, on the ground, where they were located. The head of the General Staff, through its orders, settled the procedure of how this equipment could be handed over and issued to the units, how the units could be issued the materiel they required. But I can recognise the signature of General Kukanjac, or, rather, he initialed this, his initials, as chief of the General Staff, although General Kukanjac himself took over his duties only at the beginning of 1992. So the 30th of December should not be misleading as the date here -- the 31st of December, and the fact that his initials were on this document, the fact that he initialed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 21, please. Yes. This one is the document I was reading from earlier. Superficially similar, I suppose, in appearance but with an earlier date of 31st of December, 1991. Sorry. Another one. 7th of April, 1992. 7th of April, 1992: "In accordance with Article 46 of the Temporary Rulebook... time of peace, the Article 9 of the Rulebook on the jurisdiction..." Order, this time coming from Vladan Sljivic, general colonel for SSNO logistics assistant, and he orders: "That the logistics security of all units and institutions on the territory of RS Krajina that is under the control of 'UNPROFOR' should prepare for their relocation to new areas ..." Next paragraph, paragraph 2: "Forming of the Main Staff Logistic Base of RS Krajina and zone logistic bases and reinforcement of their formations ... in accordance with the request of GSTO of RS Krajina ..." And then down to paragraph 4: "In cooperation with SSNO personnel management, the sanitary management will bring appropriate decision about the health insurance of AVL, GL, and PVL ..." What does this tell us, very briefly, about logistic support coming to RS Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formation of the logistics base for the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. That's what it tells us about, that this kind of army institution did not exist in that territory previously. The logistics base is a very complex logistic institution with -- which implies numerous material and materiel and repair capacities, and it comes under the Territorial Defence which will remain in the area under the control of the international forces. And it is regulated, in point 4, with the -- it says here sanitary management of persons and health insurance of persons who remain on the territory of the Republika Srpska Krajina. And as far as I know, this health insurance and management was done in medical military institutions, at the Medical Military Academy as well, and the costs of treatment and health care for these persons was paid for. So this is all a preparatory stage, in fact, for placing the whole -- the entire Territorial Defence, according to all the principles defined, in the territory of Krajina when UNPROFOR arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally on this exercise, Exhibit 352, tab 157. This is again outside your period, the 23rd of December, 1993, from Milan Celeketic, a colonel, 18th Corps Command of the SVK, I assume, and it says: "Order on the method of securing materials from the FRY army." "In spite of orders and many warnings that the securing of material and supplies from the VJ be done in planned fashion and through the Serbian army of Krajina Main Staff, there are instances of commands or individuals directly contacting the General Staff of the VJ or individual units. "Direct contacts give the impression of unorganised and haphazard work and incur unnecessary costs ..." And then there's an order that requests for replenishment of units that have been sent directly to the corps command, forbidding subordinate commands to approach the General Staff directly. Any comment on this? It's self-evident that it's revealing of support by the VJ of the 18th Corps Command, but any other comment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's self-evident. This is dated the 23rd of December, 1993, and it is evident from this order that there was a method of supplying the Main Staff of the army of the Republic of Krajina, and some individuals established direct links, bypassing these official channels. I assume that they must have served in the JNA and later on they were in this other army, and they used their connections in order to obtain supplies, bypassing the Main Staff. So this is actually telling them not to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go perhaps into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll just go back to that outstanding question in paragraph 78.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we've now looked at various aspects of what happened with the armies of the SVK and the VRS and their connection with the VJ. Back to a question I asked you a little earlier - my fault entirely in the way I phrased it - but as it appeared from all these various factors, were these two armies and the -- operating as if they were in different countries or in any way operating as if they were the same country? If you -- if you don't find the question helpful, say so and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered this. Objectively, there were two armies in two countries. And from a third country, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, they were treated as if they were both armies of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, because they were supplied with funds, personnel, materiel and equipment. And there is nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Can we now move to the influence, if any, of the accused over federal and Serbian institutions. In your experience, the members of the Presidency were what category or kind of politician?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - and to begin with there were eight of them - in my estimation and in the general view, were third-class cadres, third-class politicians, many of whom were not known to the general public or who were political upstarts. Real power at that time resided in the republican leaders, while the members of the Presidency were, if I can express myself metaphorically, ambassadors representing their own republics and provinces in the Presidency. In other words, they were bound to advocate the positions set by the republics. That's my impression of the members of the Presidency and its actual power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The position of the accused in this structure as you describe it was what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he -- his position was any different than that of the presidents of the other republics, but there is no doubt that he was a very strong political leader, that he was very authoritative, and that because of this, he was, in reality, able to influence four of the members of the Presidency, and these were the ones from Serbia, from Kosovo, and Metohija, and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your superior, Kadijevic, was he technically subordinated to the accused or not? We know the answer but please confirm it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither in technical terms nor in any other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 88. Did the accused exercise any influence over the appointment of people to the Serbian Ministry of the Interior? He obviously had the power to, but did he actually exercise that power?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure of appointing ministers in the government is clear. They were nominated by the Prime Minister designate, and I think that there is no doubt that in relation to the key positions, one of which was always the post of Minister of the Interior, were certainly strongly influenced by the accused. The appointees were people he had special confidence in. However, the entire procedure, in formal terms, went through the Assembly or the parliament, and there the Socialist Party of Serbia held the majority, and he was the president of that party, so that it was very easy for votes to be in favour of what had already been planned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Radmilo Bogdanovic was Minister of Internal Affairs for Serbia until March 1991, being replaced by Zoran Sokolovic, who was in office throughout the conflict. Was that replacement a genuine replacement; i.e., did Sokolovic really take over the powers of the Minister of Internal Affairs with Bogdanovic leaving the scene, or did Bogdanovic remain an influential figure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that both statements are correct. Zoran Sokolovic took over the post of Minister of the Interior of Serbia, but a strong Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. influence on key persons in the ministry was still exerted by the former minister, Radmilo Bogdanovic. Zoran Sokolovic was by nature, by character and temperament, a quiet man, and he seemed to be more of a figurehead in all this. Real power at that time, objectively within the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, resided in the head of the public -- of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness would prefer to go into closed session for what follows.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Vojna Linija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're now coming up to quarter to. We have to be out literally in two minutes. If you're going to go on to a new subject, it may be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm entirely in the Court's hands. It's a short paragraph, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We've got literally a minute, so we need to be off. Mr. Vasiljevic, would you be back, please, on Wednesday morning to continue your evidence.
